title: Good Gifts and Trained Godliness
summary: Paul exposes a demonic asceticism that forbade marriage and God-given food, then charges Timothy to teach, train in godliness, and persevere.
historicalContext: Timothy remained at Ephesus to restrain teachers who were drawing believers into speculation, myths, and quarrels (1:3–7). Chapter 4 names one concrete form their error had taken: a rigorist program that treated marriage and certain foods as spiritually defiling. Ideas that despised the material world and the body circulated widely in the first-century Greek world and would later harden into elaborate systems that made renunciation the ladder to holiness. Ephesus also prized its gymnasia, where young men trained for the city’s athletic festivals, which helps explain Paul’s vivid exercise imagery. Timothy himself was younger than many of the elders he was to guide, so his teaching risked being dismissed. Paul writes while hoping to return soon (3:14; 4:13), equipping his delegate to lead a congregation through prophecy-foretold apostasy with Scripture, example, and steady perseverance.
literaryContext: The chapter follows directly on the confession of 3:16, where the “mystery of godliness” is summed up in Christ manifested in flesh and received in glory. Chapter 4 sets that true godliness against its counterfeit. Verses 1–5 describe the coming departure, its demonic source, its hypocritical spokesmen, and its two prohibitions, answering them from creation, thanksgiving, and the word of God. Verses 6–10 turn to Timothy as a good servant who is nourished on sound teaching, refuses fables, and trains for a godliness that carries promise for both lives, anchored in hope toward the living God. Verses 11–16 gather personal charges about example, public reading and teaching, the gift received at his commissioning, visible progress, and perseverance. The word “these things” recurs (4:6, 11, 15) and ties the instruction together, while the closing promise of salvation answers the opening warning of departure.
themes: Apostasy foretold by the Spirit and fueled by deception
The goodness of God’s created gifts received with thanksgiving
Food and marriage sanctified by God’s word and prayer
Training for godliness rather than ascetic display
Hope in the living God as the motive for labor
A minister’s example, public reading of Scripture, and perseverance

outline.title: The Departure and Its False Austerity
outline.summary: The Spirit foretells apostasy driven by deceiving spirits; its teachers forbid marriage and foods God created, which His word and prayer sanctify.

outline.title: A Good Servant Trained in Godliness
outline.summary: Timothy is to teach these truths, feed on sound doctrine, refuse fables, and train for godliness in hope toward the living God.

outline.title: Example, Scripture, Gift, and Perseverance
outline.summary: Paul charges Timothy to lead by example, devote himself to Scripture and teaching, use his gift, and persevere for his own and his hearers’ salvation.

verses.bibleText: Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The small word “Now” turns from the confession that closed chapter 3 to the threat that would oppose it. The church had just been called “the pillar and ground of the truth,” and its creed had been sung as the mystery of godliness revealed in Christ. Paul immediately warns that this truth will be contested from within. He grounds the warning in the Spirit, who “speaketh expressly,” that is, in plain and unmistakable terms. Jesus had foretold false prophets who would deceive many (Matthew 24:11, 24), and Paul himself had told the Ephesian elders at Miletus that grievous wolves would come and that some of their own number would draw disciples after them (Acts 20:29–30). Whether the Spirit spoke through those earlier words or through prophets in the congregation, the matter was not left vague.

“In the latter times” points to the seasons following the prediction. The verb is future, yet verses 3–6 show that the danger was already active at Ephesus. Prophecy often speaks this way: what is foretold has begun in the prophet’s own day and will gather strength as history moves toward its close. Paul elsewhere describes a great falling away that must come before the day of Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so every generation of believers must watch, and the last generation most of all.

“Some shall depart from the faith.” The definite article points to the body of truth just confessed in 3:16. Apostasy is the movement of people who once stood inside the church and now step away from its foundation. Such departures are rarely announced as rejection; they usually arrive as refinements, deeper spirituality, or stricter devotion.

The root cause lies behind the human teachers. The apostates give heed to “seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils,” attaching themselves to teaching whose real origin is demonic. The conflict between Christ and Satan reaches into the church’s classroom. The Spirit of truth speaks clearly; the deceiving spirits lead astray. Scripture warns that such deception can include voices claiming to bring knowledge from the dead, and it directs God’s people “to the law and to the testimony” (Isaiah 8:19–20). The safeguard is to test every spirit by God’s revealed word (1 John 4:1).

wordNotes.term: ῥητῶς (rhētōs) — expressly
wordNotes.explanation: This adverb, found only here in the New Testament, means “in stated terms” or “explicitly.” Paul stresses that the coming departure was not a guess or a mood of pessimism. The Spirit had announced it plainly, so the church should not be surprised or unsettled when it appeared.

wordNotes.term: ἀποστήσονται (apostēsontai) — shall depart
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to stand away from or withdraw. Its related noun is used for the great “falling away” of 2 Thessalonians 2:3. The word assumes a former position inside the faith; it describes people who abandon ground they once occupied, which makes their influence on others especially dangerous.

verses.bibleText: Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The demonic teaching reaches the church through human voices. The Greek reads more literally “in the hypocrisy of liars,” describing the people through whom the deceiving spirits work. These teachers did not appear as enemies of godliness. Their austerity, their refusals, and their talk of higher purity made them look more devoted than ordinary believers. That outward show is the hypocrisy. A message whose origin was demonic came dressed in the costume of strict holiness, which is why it could win a hearing.

The second phrase explains how such people could teach falsehood without alarm: they had “their conscience seared with a hot iron.” The image comes from cauterizing, burning flesh until it no longer feels. A conscience treated this way stops warning. It may also suggest the branding of a slave, marking the person as belonging to another master, but the medical sense fits the context best. Paul elsewhere describes people who, “being past feeling,” gave themselves over to sin (Ephesians 4:19).

The word “their own” sharpens the tragedy. The faculty God gave each person to judge right from wrong has been disabled in the very people who claim to lead others into holiness. Throughout this letter Paul ties sound faith to a good conscience (1:5, 19; 3:9). Some had already thrust conscience aside and made shipwreck of faith. Here the end of that road appears: teachers who no longer sense that their teaching is false.

Such searing is rarely sudden. It develops as warnings are ignored again and again until the voice of conscience grows faint. Scripture urges believers to exhort one another daily so that none is hardened through the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). A tender conscience is preserved by answering God’s word promptly while it still speaks.

wordNotes.term: κεκαυστηριασμένων τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν (kekaustēriasmenōn tēn idian syneidēsin) — having their conscience seared
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle describes a completed condition with lasting effect. The verb refers to burning with a hot iron, whether to deaden tissue or to brand. In context the stress falls on insensitivity: their own moral judge no longer protests against the falsehood they teach, so their deception includes self-deception.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων (en hypokrisei pseudologōn) — speaking lies in hypocrisy
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase names the human channel of the demonic teaching: liars acting a part. “Hypocrisy” originally referred to playing a role on stage. Their show of rigorous devotion masked a message that contradicted the truth of God.

verses.bibleText: Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now names the two practical demands of the false teachers. First, they were “forbidding to marry.” Marriage belongs to God’s design from the beginning, when He declared that it was not good for the man to be alone and joined husband and wife as one flesh (Genesis 2:18, 24). Paul valued singleness as a calling that can free a person for undivided service (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35), yet he insisted that those who marry do not sin (1 Corinthians 7:28). This same letter expects overseers and deacons to be faithful husbands (3:2, 12) and counsels younger widows to marry (5:14). To prohibit marriage as defiling is to accuse the Creator of giving something unclean.

Second, they were “commanding to abstain from meats.” The Greek word is general, meaning foods, though it may point particularly to flesh foods. Such teaching likely rested on a view that matter and the body are inferior or evil, so holiness would increase as one withdrew from bodily things. Paul had confronted similar rules in Colossae, “touch not; taste not; handle not,” which appear wise but have no value against the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:21–23). Later centuries would see the same impulse elevated into enforced celibacy and rules of abstinence presented as a higher path to God.

Paul’s answer is precise: these are foods “which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving.” The phrase defines the scope of his argument. He defends what God made for human use. From the beginning God specified food for humanity (Genesis 1:29). After the Flood He permitted flesh food, while the distinction between clean and unclean animals was already known (Genesis 7:2; 9:3), and the law later set out which creatures were to be eaten (Leviticus 11). The false teachers forbade what God had given; Paul does not answer by permitting what God had withheld. The passage therefore does not abolish the clean and unclean distinction. It opposes an asceticism that refused God’s gifts.

Those who “believe and know the truth” are the people best placed to enjoy these gifts. Knowing the Creator through His word, they understand both what He has provided and the gratitude with which it should be received. Their table becomes a place of trust rather than suspicion.

wordNotes.term: κωλυόντων γαμεῖν, ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων (kōlyontōn gamein, apechesthai brōmatōn) — forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats
wordNotes.explanation: The Greek uses one verb, “forbidding,” for two clauses, so a second verb such as “commanding” must be supplied before “to abstain,” as the KJV does. The noun for “meats” means food in general, though in debates elsewhere it can stand for flesh food. Both prohibitions treated good gifts as spiritually dangerous.

wordNotes.term: εἰς μετάλημψιν μετὰ εὐχαριστίας (eis metalēmpsin meta eucharistias) — to be received with thanksgiving
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase states the Creator’s purpose: these foods were made for sharing and partaking, and the fitting response is gratitude. The emphasis falls on God’s intention. What He created as food is to be accepted thankfully, which rules out treating it as defiling.

verses.bibleText: For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul supplies the principle behind his answer: “every creature of God is good.” The words echo the verdict of creation week, when God saw everything He had made and declared it very good (Genesis 1:31). Teachers who regarded the material world as an obstacle to holiness were contradicting the first chapter of Scripture. Matter is not the enemy. Sin, not the body or its appetites as God designed them, is what corrupts human life.

The statement must be read within the argument. “Every creature” refers back to the things just named in verse 3: the foods God created to be received, along with marriage. Paul is not claiming that every living thing is food. A creature can be wholly good for the purpose God gave it without being given for the table. The same Creator who pronounced His works good also distinguished clean from unclean animals before Sinai (Genesis 7:2) and later set out which were food in Leviticus 11. An argument from creation cannot overturn the Creator’s own designations, and the Bible nowhere withdraws that distinction. This verse, then, does not abolish the clean and unclean distinction; it denies that God’s gifts are evil.

“And nothing to be refused.” The rare word means something thrown away as worthless or taboo. Ascetic religion treats God’s gifts as contaminating, and so it implies a grudging God who gives with one hand and condemns with the other. Paul paints the opposite picture of a generous Giver from whom every good and perfect gift comes down (James 1:17).

The condition is “if it be received with thanksgiving.” Gratitude acknowledges the Giver and keeps the gift in its place. A person who eats with thanks is not indulging appetite for its own sake, nor fearing the food as defiling, but receiving from God’s hand. This also shapes the practice of healthful living. Care in what one eats is stewardship of a body that belongs to God, offered “to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31), never a ladder of merit.

wordNotes.term: πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ καλόν (pan ktisma theou kalon) — every creature of God is good
wordNotes.explanation: “Creature” here means a created thing. The adjective “good” describes what is fitting and excellent for its purpose. In context the phrase refers to the foods and the marriage just defended, and it affirms the goodness of creation against those who despised the material world.

wordNotes.term: οὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον (ouden apoblēton) — nothing to be refused
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective, found only here in the New Testament, describes something cast away as rejected. Paul denies that God’s created gifts are to be shunned as polluting. Thankful reception, not ritual avoidance of what God has given, marks the believer’s relationship to them.

verses.bibleText: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” To sanctify is to set apart for holy use. Paul does not mean that a meal becomes sacred in some ritual sense; he means that it is placed rightly within a life devoted to God and declared fit for use by the Giver Himself.

Two means accomplish this. The first is “the word of God,” what God has spoken about His gifts. Creation itself began with His word assigning food to humanity (Genesis 1:29–30), and Scripture went on to designate which creatures were food (Leviticus 11). The word of God sanctifies food, then, by identifying it as His gift and appointing its use. This is why the passage does not abolish the clean and unclean distinction: the very word that sanctifies food is the word that marked out clean from unclean. Prayer cannot set apart as food what God’s word has never given for that purpose.

The second means is prayer. The term can describe petition in general, but here it carries the tone of thanksgiving already stressed twice. Jesus gave thanks before He broke bread for the multitudes (Mark 8:6), and Paul did the same aboard the storm-tossed ship (Acts 27:35). Thanks at the table confesses that daily provision comes from God and turns an ordinary meal into an act of worship.

The same principle applies to marriage, the other gift the false teachers forbade. Marriage too rests on God’s word at creation and is honored when received with prayer and gratitude (Hebrews 13:4).

The whole of life can be lived in this way. “Whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks” (Colossians 3:17). The believer does not escape holiness by retreating from the material world. Holiness enters the kitchen, the table, and the home when God’s word directs and grateful prayer receives.

wordNotes.term: ἁγιάζεται (hagiazetai) — it is sanctified
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to set apart or treat as holy. Applied to food, it describes being consecrated for proper use within a life belonging to God. The present tense suggests a continual reality whenever the gift is received according to God’s word and with prayer.

wordNotes.term: διὰ λόγου θεοῦ καὶ ἐντεύξεως (dia logou theou kai enteuxeōs) — by the word of God and prayer
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase joins an objective and a subjective means. The word of God supplies what He has declared about His gifts, including which creatures are food; prayer supplies the believer’s grateful response. The noun for prayer (used also in 2:1) here leans toward thanksgiving.

verses.bibleText: If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from the false teachers to Timothy’s own task. “If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things” uses a verb meaning to lay something before others, to set it out for their consideration. The tone is pastoral rather than harsh. Timothy is to place the truths of verses 1–5 before the congregation so that believers recognize the error and understand why God’s gifts are good. The hearers are “the brethren,” members of the household of God (3:15) who need instruction more than denunciation.

The one who does this is “a good minister of Jesus Christ.” The word minister is the ordinary term for a servant. Timothy’s worth is measured by faithful service to his Master, not by originality or popularity.

The servant who feeds others must himself be fed. He is “nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine.” The present participle pictures continuous nourishment, a daily diet rather than an occasional meal. “The words of faith” are the content of the Christian message, and “good doctrine” is the teaching that stands opposite the “doctrines of devils” in verse 1. A minister who stops eating soon has nothing wholesome to offer, and no one can be nourished by food that someone else has eaten.

“Whereunto thou hast attained” could be rendered “which you have closely followed.” Timothy had been taught the Scriptures from childhood and had walked alongside Paul for years (2 Timothy 3:10, 14–15). His defence against novelty was steady, positive grounding in what he had already received. Error is answered most effectively when truth is set out clearly and lived consistently.

wordNotes.term: διάκονος (diakonos) — minister
wordNotes.explanation: The word means servant and can describe table service, ministry in general, or the office of deacon (3:8–13). Here it describes Timothy’s role as one who leads by serving Christ and His people. Jesus defined greatness in His kingdom by this very word.

wordNotes.term: ἐντρεφόμενος (entrephomenos) — nourished up
wordNotes.explanation: This participle, used only here in the New Testament, means being reared or trained in something. The present tense signals an ongoing process. Timothy’s capacity to teach depends on his continuing to feed on the words of the faith.

verses.bibleText: But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But refuse profane and old wives’ fables.” The verb means to decline or have nothing to do with. Timothy does not need to chase down every speculation in order to refute it point by point. Some ideas deserve a firm refusal. These fables are “profane,” common and empty of anything holy, however spiritual their vocabulary may sound. They are also “old wives’” tales, an expression used in the ancient world for credulous stories told without evidence. The phrase is a cutting idiom, not a slight on older women, whom Timothy is to honor as mothers (5:2). The myths are likely related to the endless genealogies and speculations already mentioned in 1:4.

The positive charge follows: “exercise thyself rather unto godliness.” The verb is drawn from the gymnasium, where athletes trained with discipline and sweat. Ephesus was proud of its training grounds, and the image would be vivid. Paul has just rejected an asceticism that punished the body, yet he does not replace it with spiritual ease. Godliness must be trained. Prayer, attention to Scripture, self-control, and obedient habits are exercised until they become strong.

Such training is not a human attempt to earn grace. God works in His people both to will and to do, and they work out what He works in (Philippians 2:12–13). Discipline is the form grace takes in a life that is growing.

wordNotes.term: γραώδεις μύθους (graōdeis mythous) — old wives’ fables
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective, found only here in the New Testament, described stories fit for credulous gossip. Combined with “myths,” it dismisses the false teaching as frivolous and baseless. The wording reflects a common idiom for empty tales rather than a judgment on any group of people.

wordNotes.term: γύμναζε σεαυτόν (gymnaze seauton) — exercise thyself
wordNotes.explanation: The present imperative calls for continual training. The verb comes from athletic practice and is used figuratively in the New Testament for the shaping of moral and spiritual capacities. Godliness is both the goal of training and the sphere in which it takes place.

verses.bibleText: For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul explains why training in godliness matters by comparing it with another kind of training. “Bodily exercise profiteth little.” The phrase could refer to the austerities of the false teachers, but the athletic image of verse 7 makes literal physical training the more natural sense. Paul has already rejected the ascetic program outright; it would be strange to grant it even a little value here. Athletic training does profit. It strengthens the body and serves health. Its reach, however, is limited in scope and in time, for it serves only the present life.

This is no dismissal of care for the body. The body is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and wise habits of exercise, rest, and diet are part of faithful stewardship. A healthy body can make a clearer mind and a more useful servant. Paul’s point is comparative. When physical discipline becomes an end in itself, it crowds out what matters most.

“But godliness is profitable unto all things.” Reverent devotion to God shapes every relationship, every decision, every season. It also carries a promise: it has “promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.” In this life it brings the life of fellowship with God, peace, and purpose, even amid hardship. Jesus promised those who leave all for Him a hundredfold now and eternal life in the world to come (Mark 10:29–30). The life to come is given in full when Christ returns and raises His people, putting on them the immortality they do not possess by nature.

A balanced Christian will therefore keep the body fit for service without letting the gym, the scale, or a regimen measure spiritual worth. Training in godliness is the exercise that lasts.

wordNotes.term: σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον (sōmatikē gymnasia pros oligon) — bodily exercise profiteth little
wordNotes.explanation: The noun for exercise appears only here in the New Testament and refers to physical training. The phrase “for little” indicates limited benefit, both in extent and in duration. Paul does not call it useless; he sets its modest value beside the unlimited value of godliness.

wordNotes.term: εὐσέβεια (eusebeia) — godliness
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes reverence toward God expressed in a life that honors Him. In the Pastoral Epistles it is rooted in the mystery revealed in Christ (3:16) and carries inner power, not mere outward form. It is a key word of this letter.

verses.bibleText: This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.” Paul uses this formula five times in the Pastoral Epistles to commend a reliable statement that was probably circulating among the churches (1:15; 3:1; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). The same full wording appeared in 1:15, where it introduced the gospel summary that Christ came to save sinners.

The saying most likely points back to verse 8. Its balanced, proverbial shape suits a remembered maxim, and verse 10 then reads as Paul’s personal endorsement of it. Some connect the formula instead to the hope in verse 10. Either way the content is weighty: godliness carries the promise of life now and forever.

“Worthy of all acceptation” calls for wholehearted reception. A true saying can be admired without being embraced. Paul asks Timothy and the church to receive this one fully, letting it reorder their priorities and their effort. Such sayings also served the churches as compact anchors, easy to remember and repeat when novel teaching pressed in.

wordNotes.term: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος (pistos ho logos kai pasēs apodochēs axios) — a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation
wordNotes.explanation: “Faithful” means trustworthy, able to bear weight. “Acceptation” is the welcome given to something received gladly. The added phrase urges personal and complete acceptance, not merely agreement that the saying is correct.

verses.bibleText: For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For therefore,” meaning “to this end,” connects Paul’s labor with the promise of life just affirmed. Because godliness has a future, he and his colleagues pour themselves out. “We both labour” uses a verb for toil to the point of weariness. Paul knew the cost of ministry in sleepless nights, hunger, and danger (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The KJV continues “and suffer reproach,” while many ancient manuscripts read “and strive,” a word from athletic contest. Both describe the same life: strenuous effort in the face of opposition.

The reason is hope: “because we trust in the living God.” The perfect tense suggests a settled hope that continues. He is “the living God,” in contrast to the lifeless idols that crowded Ephesus and to the empty fables of verse 7. Only a living God can give the life promised in verse 8, and the God who raised Jesus from the dead guarantees that labor in His service is never wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58).

He is “the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.” Paul has already said that God wills all people to be saved and that Christ gave Himself a ransom for all (2:4–6). God’s saving purpose and provision reach every person without exception, and He sustains the life of all (Acts 17:25). Yet the phrase does not teach that every person will finally be saved. Salvation is received through faith, and those who refuse it face judgment (John 3:16–18, 36). “Specially” marks believers as the ones in whom God’s saving work comes to full effect. Some read the word as “that is,” identifying believers as the saved; on either reading, salvation belongs to those who trust Him.

This truth fuels mission. Because God offers salvation to all, His servants labor to reach all. Because it is received by faith, they call people to believe. Paul’s weariness was not the anxious striving of a man trying to secure his own standing with God; it was the energy of one whose hope was already fixed and who longed for others to share it.

wordNotes.term: σωτὴρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, μάλιστα πιστῶν (sōtēr pantōn anthrōpōn, malista pistōn) — Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe
wordNotes.explanation: “Saviour” is a favorite title for God in these letters. The universal phrase echoes 2:4–6, where God desires all to be saved. The adverb “specially” either singles out believers within that universal offer or defines the saved as those who believe. Both readings exclude universalism, because salvation is enjoyed through faith.

wordNotes.term: ἠλπίκαμεν ἐπὶ θεῷ ζῶντι (ēlpikamen epi theō zōnti) — we trust in the living God
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect tense means “we have set our hope and keep it set.” Hope in the New Testament combines confident expectation with patient trust. Its object is the living God, the source and giver of life, which makes the promise of verse 8 secure.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These things command and teach.” The short verse gathers up what precedes and prepares for the personal charges that follow. “These things” refers chiefly to the truths of verses 6–10: the goodness of God’s gifts, the priority of godliness, and hope in the living God who saves.

The two verbs work together. To command is to give authoritative instruction, the same language Paul used when he left Timothy at Ephesus to “charge some that they teach no other doctrine” (1:3). To teach is to explain and ground that instruction so that hearers understand it. Command without teaching becomes mere pressure; teaching without command becomes mere discussion. Both are present imperatives, calling for continual practice.

Timothy’s authority is borrowed. The apostle of Christ Jesus commissions the servant of Christ Jesus to pass on what has been entrusted to him. That authority would soon be tested, as the next verse shows, because the one giving the charge was younger than many who would hear it.

wordNotes.term: παράγγελλε καὶ δίδασκε (parangelle kai didaske) — command and teach
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb was used for orders passed down a chain of authority, as from a commander to troops. The second describes instruction that explains truth. The pairing presents Timothy as both a delegated authority and a patient teacher.

verses.bibleText: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Let no man despise thy youth.” The word for youth could describe a person up to about forty years of age. Timothy had served with Paul for more than a decade and was probably in his thirties, yet in a culture that honored age he would be giving instruction to elders older than himself. Some might look down on him and dismiss his teaching.

Paul’s remedy is to “be thou an example of the believers.” The phrase may mean an example for believers to follow, a pattern stamped out for others to imitate. Authority in the church is earned and sustained by character.

Paul lists the areas of example. “In word” refers to speech, both public teaching and private conversation. “In conversation” in the KJV means manner of life, the whole pattern of conduct. These two cover the outward life. “In charity” is love, the first mark of a disciple. “In spirit” is absent from many ancient manuscripts; where it stands it may refer to the disposition and fervor of one led by the Spirit. “In faith” describes trust in God and faithfulness that others can rely on. “In purity” covers moral cleanness, especially sexual integrity, which would be vital in his relationships with younger women (5:2).

Scripture repeatedly shows God using the young when they walk faithfully (Jeremiah 1:6–8). The verse also speaks to congregations, which should judge leaders by godliness rather than by age, and to every believer, for each is watched by someone learning what a follower of Christ looks like.

wordNotes.term: τύπος (typos) — example
wordNotes.explanation: The word originally meant the impression left by a blow or a stamp. It came to mean a pattern or model. Paul uses it of himself and of churches that others should imitate. Timothy is to be a visible pattern of Christian life.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἀναστροφῇ (en anastrophē) — in conversation
wordNotes.explanation: The KJV “conversation” meant way of life, not merely talk. The Greek describes one’s conduct as one moves about in daily life. Paired with “word,” it covers both what Timothy says and how he lives.

verses.bibleText: Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Till I come” recalls Paul’s hope of returning soon (3:14). Until then Timothy must carry the central tasks of public ministry. “Give attendance to” means to devote one’s mind and effort to something, a word that implies diligent private preparation behind public work.

Three tasks follow. “Reading” refers to the public reading of Scripture in worship. The church inherited the practice from the synagogue, where the law and the prophets were read aloud each Sabbath (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:15). Few households owned scrolls, so most believers heard God’s word chiefly when it was read in the assembly. Apostolic letters were soon read the same way (Colossians 4:16).

“Exhortation” is the appeal that applies the reading to life, urging hearers to respond. In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, Paul was invited after the reading to give “any word of exhortation” (Acts 13:15). “Doctrine” is instruction that explains the content of the faith in an orderly way.

The order is instructive. Scripture comes first, then its application, then its explanation. A congregation exposed to fables needs a steady diet of God’s word read aloud, pressed on the conscience, and carefully taught. The same pattern serves the church still: worship that gives Scripture a central place forms people who can recognize error when they hear it.

wordNotes.term: τῇ ἀναγνώσει (tē anagnōsei) — to reading
wordNotes.explanation: The noun describes reading aloud, specifically the public reading of Scripture in the assembly. The article points to a recognized part of worship. Its use shows the church continuing the synagogue’s practice of hearing the written word together.

wordNotes.term: τῇ παρακλήσει, τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ (tē paraklēsei, tē didaskalia) — to exhortation, to doctrine
wordNotes.explanation: Exhortation urges and encourages, calling hearers to act on what they have heard. Doctrine is the content of teaching, explained and ordered. Together they describe preaching that both persuades the will and informs the mind.

verses.bibleText: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Neglect not the gift that is in thee.” The gift is a grace-gift from God, an equipping by the Spirit for the work to which Timothy was called. It resides in him, yet it can be neglected. God gives; the servant must use and cultivate what is given. In his second letter Paul will urge Timothy to stir up this gift, like fanning embers into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

The gift “was given thee by prophecy.” Paul has already referred to prophecies that pointed to Timothy (1:18). As the Holy Spirit once directed the church at Antioch to set apart Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3), so prophetic words had identified Timothy for his ministry.

It came “with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery,” the council of elders. Paul also laid hands on him (2 Timothy 1:6), most likely on the same occasion, with the elders joining the apostle. The laying on of hands had deep roots: Moses laid hands on Joshua before the congregation (Numbers 27:18–23), and the apostles prayed and laid hands on the seven (Acts 6:6). In such acts the church publicly recognized God’s choice, set the person apart, and prayed for him. The gift came from God, not from the hands themselves; the ceremony acknowledged and confirmed what God was doing.

Remembering that commissioning would steady Timothy when his youth was criticized. His ministry rested on God’s call, the church’s recognition, and the Spirit’s equipping. Every believer has received some gift for the good of the body, and each is accountable for its use.

wordNotes.term: χάρισμα (charisma) — gift
wordNotes.explanation: The noun is built on the word for grace and denotes a gift freely bestowed. Paul uses it for the varied endowments by which the Spirit equips believers for service. Its origin in grace excludes boasting, while its presence calls for faithful use.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου (tou presbyteriou) — of the presbytery
wordNotes.explanation: The term refers to a body of elders. Elsewhere in the New Testament it names the council of Jewish elders in Jerusalem. Here it describes the Christian elders who joined in recognizing and commissioning Timothy.

verses.bibleText: Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Meditate upon these things.” The verb can mean to ponder carefully or to practice diligently, and both senses fit. Timothy is to think about these charges until they shape his mind, and to work at them until they become second nature. The same word appears in the Greek Old Testament for the righteous person who meditates in God’s law day and night (Psalm 1:2).

“Give thyself wholly to them” translates a compact phrase, literally “be in them.” Timothy is to be absorbed in his calling, immersed in it the way a person lives within the air he breathes. Divided attention would weaken his ministry.

The purpose follows: “that thy profiting may appear to all.” The word means progress or advance. Timothy is not required to appear flawless; he is to grow, and the growth should be evident. Visible progress in faith, love, and purity would answer those who despised his youth more convincingly than any defense. A congregation can trust a leader whose life keeps moving toward Christ.

wordNotes.term: μελέτα (meleta) — meditate
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative means to attend to with care, whether by thinking it through or by practicing it. In the Greek Psalter it describes meditation on God’s law. Paul calls for focused, sustained attention to the charges of this chapter.

wordNotes.term: ἡ προκοπή (hē prokopē) — profiting
wordNotes.explanation: The noun means progress or advancement. Paul uses it for the advance of the gospel and for believers’ progress in faith. It assumes a journey under way and growth that others can see.

verses.bibleText: Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter closes with a summary charge. “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine.” Timothy must keep close watch over two things: his own life and his teaching. The order matters. Paul had told the Ephesian elders at Miletus, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Acts 20:28). A teacher whose life contradicts his message undermines it, and sound teaching from a careless life rarely persuades. Yet character cannot replace truth either. Timothy must guard what he teaches as carefully as how he lives.

“Continue in them.” The verb means to remain or persevere. The false teachers had departed (v. 1); Timothy must stay. Perseverance is the steady faithfulness of someone who keeps walking in the way he has begun, year after year. It is not a matter of earning God’s favor but of refusing to let go of grace already received, like the good ground that holds the word fast and bears fruit with patience (Luke 8:15).

“For in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.” The language is strong but not strange. God alone is the Saviour (v. 10), and salvation is by grace through faith. Yet Scripture also speaks of human beings as instruments in saving others (Romans 11:14; 1 Corinthians 9:22; James 5:20). Timothy saves himself by continuing in the faith that receives God’s grace, for faith that perseveres is faith that endures to the end (Colossians 1:22–23). He saves his hearers by faithfully placing before them the truth through which God brings people to salvation.

The chapter began with some who would depart from the faith and ends with the promise of salvation for those who remain in it. Between those two lies the steady work of a servant: feeding on the word, training in godliness, living as an example, and keeping watch. The stakes are eternal, and the means are ordinary faithfulness sustained by the living God.

wordNotes.term: ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ καὶ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ (epeche seautō kai tē didaskalia) — take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to fix one’s attention on something and keep it there. Timothy must watch both his own life and the content of his teaching. The repeated “thyself” in this verse places personal faithfulness alongside doctrinal faithfulness.

wordNotes.term: ἐπίμενε αὐτοῖς … σώσεις (epimene autois … sōseis) — continue in them … thou shalt save
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb calls for perseverance; Paul uses it elsewhere for continuing in God’s kindness and in the faith. The future “shalt save” describes final salvation, experienced by those who continue and shared with hearers who receive the truth.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why might a religion of strict renunciation look holier than a life of grateful obedience, and what does it reveal about our picture of God?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: True godliness receives God’s good gifts with thanksgiving under the direction of His word, trains the whole life toward Christlikeness, and perseveres in sound teaching that leads to salvation.
importantTerms: sanctified by the word of God
discussionQuestions: How does Paul’s appeal to creation answer teachers who treated marriage and food as defiling?
Why does Paul limit his statement to foods God created to be received, and how does that bear on the clean and unclean distinction?
What is the difference between training for godliness and the bodily austerity Paul rejects?
How can a younger leader earn the hearing that age alone does not supply?
In what sense can a teacher “save” himself and his hearers?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 4 does not declare every creature edible; it defends the foods God created for human use, as His word designates them, and does not abolish the clean and unclean distinction.
Prayer over a meal is not a formula that turns what Scripture forbids into food.
“Bodily exercise profiteth little” does not dismiss care for the body, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit.
“Saviour of all men” does not teach that everyone will finally be saved; salvation is received by faith.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the goodness of creation and the authority of Scripture: the Creator’s gifts are received gratefully, and His word defines both what they are and how they are used.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive every gift of God with thanks, train your life toward godliness, and keep close watch on your life and your teaching so that others may be helped toward Christ.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The living God, Creator of every good gift, is the Saviour who offers life to all and grants it to those who believe.
flow: God created the world good and gives His gifts to be received with thanksgiving.
Deception persuades people that holiness comes through self-made rules and harshness toward the body.
The living God is the Saviour whose grace reaches every kind of person.
Salvation is received by trusting Him, and that trust is trained into a godly life.
Godliness carries a promise for the present life and for the life to come.
simpleIllustrations: A gift received with a thank-you note honors the giver; one hidden away out of suspicion insults him.
An athlete’s training shapes a body for a season of competition, while training in godliness shapes a person for eternity.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you set your hope on the living God who offers you life now and life in the age to come?
cautions: Do not present healthful living as a way to earn salvation; it is grateful stewardship of God’s gifts.
Do not use 4:4 to dismiss the biblical distinction between clean and unclean foods.
Do not imply that God’s desire to save all means all will be saved apart from faith.

reflectionQuestions: Do I receive food, rest, and relationships as gifts from a generous Creator, and do I thank Him for them?
Where am I tempted to measure holiness by outward severity rather than by love, faith, and purity?
What does my daily routine show about whether I am training for godliness or only for this life?
Is my conscience still tender to God’s word, or have I grown used to ignoring its warnings?
Whose example am I shaping by my speech and conduct, and what are they learning from it?
